title: Christ the Head and the Veiling of Women
english: But we shall not follow their foolishness. How could we? We believe that the Word who sprang from the Father is uncreated, as being from an uncreated Father. And we say that He has been called the head of every man (1 Corinthians 11:3), as the archetype, as I said; but since He appeared as man in the last times of the age, and as one of the same kind as men in His humanity, He was given as head to the Church, which is His body (Ephesians 1:22–23). For He holds the first place in all things, as Paul says (Colossians 1:18).
“Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head,” and so on (1 Corinthians 11:4).

Do you see how he makes the law of nature the judge and arbiter of what befits each? For openness is most fitting for men, while for a woman being veiled is an adornment. So the unseemliness of the image would quite reasonably be an insult to the archetype. For if man is the image and glory of God (1 Corinthians 11:7), as according to the Scriptures he was made (Genesis 1:27), let him keep before God the openness that befits him, with his head uncovered, since nature does not reproach him for having to go uncovered. For the Divine is free and beyond all blame, rich in its own glory and held in wonder.

And if woman is in the likeness of man, an image of an image and a glory of a glory, and nature also lays it down for her to wear long hair (1 Corinthians 11:15), why should what comes second in grace contend with what is first? For she too is according to the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), but as it were through the mediation of man, so that in some small respect she differs in nature. I will not bring a charge against her when she wraps her person in modesty as far as she can and crowns it with her hair; for to go openly uncovered is not without harm for women.

So, he says, let her be veiled because of the angels (1 Corinthians 11:10), clearly meaning those whom God has stationed in the churches. Not that they suffer anything in seeing women. Human beings, who have this coarse body taken from the earth and are pushed down toward baser things by inborn pleasures, might suffer harm, being stirred by the beauty of women toward what is not fitting. But as for the holy angels, what could anyone think or say of that kind? For they are holy and above all defilement, since they are outside the flesh and have bodies that are fine and spiritual, beyond the grasp of the human mind. Rather, it is because they are deeply grieved if anyone neglects the law of what is fitting.

And being veiled befits women, and nature is witness to this: “for her hair,” he says, “has been given to her as a covering” (1 Corinthians 11:15). So let what is fitting be kept in this matter too, because of those who know the will of the Creator better than we do.

The inspired Paul uses yet another skilful device. He said that man was made according to the image and likeness of God, and he plainly insisted that the female has been cast, as it were, behind his honor and glory, adding what follows: “For woman,” he says, “is the glory of man; for man was not created for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man” (1 Corinthians 11:7, 9). Then, gently covering over what would likely grieve women, he goes on to say, “Nevertheless, neither is woman without man, nor man without woman” (1 Corinthians 11:11).

For woman admittedly came from man, and this is true (1 Corinthians 11:12); yet she has been found to have her share in bringing man into being. Nature, bringing both together into one, has made them need each other, wisely binding them together in love. And he further confirms that God is the Creator of all things, saying, “But all things are from God” (1 Corinthians 11:12); for all things were brought into being through Christ (John 1:3).
Tome Five. Discourse One.

“No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus is accursed,’” and so on (1 Corinthians 12:3). Our Lord Jesus Christ promised that when He had gone away He would send us the Comforter (John 16:7), and to this He added, “He will glorify Me” (John 16:14). And we understand, quite rightly, that His Spirit glorifies Christ both by making wise those in whom He comes to dwell and by making Christ dwell in the saints through Himself; for Christ is in us through the Holy Spirit. And He glorifies Him also in another way…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74, Fragmenta in 1 Cor (Khazarzar transcription). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.

The section opens with ‘ἑψόμεθα· πόθεν;’, which completes a sentence begun at the end of the previous section (‘ἀλλ’ οὐ ταῖς ἐκείνων ἀβελτερίαις’); the whole clause (‘But we shall not follow their foolishness’) is given here.
The section ends with ‘δοξάζει δὲ καὶ’, and the next section opens with ‘ἑτέρως’; ‘in another way’ is given here before the ellipsis, so that the sentence reads whole.
ἀγένητον (single nu, ‘uncreated, not come into being’) is rendered ‘uncreated’, not ‘unbegotten’ (ἀγέννητον).
The sentence on Christ as head of the Church has no main verb in the Greek (‘… εἰς κεφαλὴν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ’). ‘He was given’ is supplied from Ephesians 1:22 (ἔδωκεν), which Cyril is quoting.
παρρησία / παρρησιάζεσθαι here means the open, uncovered head, rendered ‘openness’ and ‘to go openly uncovered’.
‘λεπτοῖς τε καὶ νοητοῖς … σώμασιν’: Cyril speaks of the angels’ ‘fine and spiritual’ bodies (νοητός, perceived by the mind rather than the senses); kept as he says it.
The PG headings ‘ΤΟΜΟΣ Ε. ΛΟΓΟΣ Α.’ are kept as one short paragraph.
‘Ἀνάθεμα Ἰησοῦν’ is rendered ‘Jesus is accursed’.

title: Jesus Is Lord: The Varieties of Gifts
english: …in another way, for the Spirit works through the hands of the saints the deeds that serve his glory. And if his Spirit glorifies the Son, how could anyone speaking in the Spirit speak evil of him? He will rather say, “Jesus is Lord” (1 Corinthians 12:3). So those who rank with creation the one through whom all things were brought into being (John 1:3) would have no share at all in the Holy Spirit, for they plainly say, “Jesus is accursed” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

But those who devoutly confess that Jesus is God and Lord will have the fact itself as witness that they have been initiated through the Spirit into the knowledge of beholding God in him. “For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). Knowing what is hidden in God, the Spirit carries it across to the souls of the saints and plants in them a knowledge free from error and beyond reproach.

And the inspired Paul himself is witness to this when he goes on to say, “Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, and the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4–6). For just as those who hold power over affairs on earth, and adorn the thrones of kingship, crown the more loyal of their own guards with different honors, so the holy and consubstantial Trinity distributes a rich possession of the good things from above to those who love it with a sound heart and a whole mind, through the one Spirit, as through Christ, from the Father. For all things are from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.
“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is profitable. For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom,” and so on (1 Corinthians 12:7–8).

For he knows, he knows the times that befit each of the things he does, he “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” as it is written (Colossians 2:3). What the gifts are, and what the distributions, and indeed the workings of miracles, Paul makes clear when he says, “For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom” (1 Corinthians 12:8). The word of wisdom, as it seems to me at least, is the word given “in the opening of the mouth” (Ephesians 6:19): ready and flowing, as if it came from a very nimble tongue.

“To another, the word of knowledge” (1 Corinthians 12:8). For there are some among us who lack readiness in speech and have not gained the freedom to express themselves with ease, yet they are very deep in understanding. They come to the sacred words most thoughtfully and with great subtlety, and they are able to lead others into the mysteries and readily lay open what they have contemplated. But both the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge are supplied through the one Spirit, from the Father through the Son, to those worthy to receive them. It is a word of knowledge when someone knows the sense of the divine oracles and is able to unfold their meaning, but cannot teach it eloquently.

Both the one and the other are supplied to the worthy through the one Spirit, from the Father through the Son, who is said to apportion the ministries (1 Corinthians 12:5). For some of the holy apostles he commanded to proclaim the word of faith to those of the blood of Israel, and others again he assigned to the lands of the Gentiles. And this too he brought about through the Holy Spirit. Indeed, in the Acts of the holy apostles we shall find it written: “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them’ ” (Acts 13:2).

The inspired Paul was appointed to the apostleship of the Gentiles, and this ministry fell to him as his lot. He will confirm it himself when he writes, “Inasmuch then as I am an apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry” (Romans 11:13). So the Son apportions the ministries, and the Holy Spirit carries the matter out with authority, for he is the Spirit of the Son. But the workings of miracles as well, that is…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74, Fragmenta in 1 Cor (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.

The section opens with ἑτέρως, “in another way,” which closes the sentence at the end of the previous section (“And He glorifies Him also in another way”). The words are given again here so that the sentence reads whole.

“Jesus is accursed” renders Ἀνάθεμα Ἰησοῦς, as in the previous section. Those who “rank with creation” the one through whom all things were made are those who count the Son among the creatures; Cyril says they in effect make that curse.

“Devoutly” renders εὐσεβῶς, which stands between the confession and the verb; it may also be read with the verb that follows (“will have the fact itself as witness”). The sense is the same: a right confession of Christ is itself the proof of the Spirit’s teaching.
“He knows, he knows” keeps Cyril’s doubled verb (οἶδεν γὰρ οἶδεν). The one meant is Christ, in whom the treasures of wisdom are hidden (Colossians 2:3).
Cyril takes the word of wisdom as ready, fluent speech, and the word of knowledge as deep understanding of Scripture without ease of speech.
The section ends mid-sentence; it continues in the next section.

title: Faith, Healings, Miracles and Tongues
english: …the divine signs done through the saints, the same God accomplishes for us (1 Corinthians 12:6). For all things, as I said, are from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and in everything that is well done the holy and consubstantial Trinity is glorified. For see how he begins from the Spirit, as the one who is in us and works the distribution of the divine gifts; then, raising his account to the Son, who is Son by nature, he goes up at last to the Father, ascribing to him, by way of the Son, the working done through the Spirit.

“To another, faith by the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:9). Faith here would be, as I think, steadfastness toward every good thing whatever, and toward whatever God may will. For in this sense we say that Moses, the revealer of holy things, was faithful “in all his house” (Hebrews 3:2; Numbers 12:7). For faith would not be understood or spoken of as only the duty to believe that by nature and in truth there is one God of all, but as standing firm in soul, “and being ready to walk with the Lord God,” in the words of the prophet (Micah 6:8). And so the inspired disciples once came to Christ, saying plainly, “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5).

Besides this, gifts of healing are also given by the one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:9). And again, mark this closely, I ask you: though the Spirit is said to distribute the gifts of healing, it is Christ who gives them. For he gave the holy apostles “authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out” (Matthew 10:1); and indeed he said, “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without cost; give without cost” (Matthew 10:8).

The workings of miracles are certainly his as well, but in the one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:10). For instance, Moses threw his staff on the ground and it became a serpent (Exodus 4:3); he turned the rivers into blood (Exodus 7:20); he brought water out of the rock (Exodus 17:6). And the blessed prophets performed a great many deeds beyond words and beyond wonder. These, we say, are the workings of miracles through the one Spirit. Another, again, prophesies, but not apart from the Spirit; and someone has the discernment of spirits, but in the Spirit himself (1 Corinthians 12:10). What kind of spirits are meant has been said earlier.

Paul also insists that to others it is given to know kinds of tongues, and indeed their interpretation (1 Corinthians 12:10). This we call a gift of its own kind, supplied to some in God’s plan, at a set time and for a need. But some spoke in the tongues though they had not known them before, while others understood and interpreted them, though some of them had never before had an ear trained in such languages or used to them. Yet the inspired Paul firmly states that speaking in tongues was given to the believers of that time not as counted among the gifts but as ranking as a sign. And he set beside it a prophetic oracle that runs thus: “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of others I will speak to this people, and not even so will they believe” (1 Corinthians 14:21; Isaiah 28:11–12).

The Spirit works the distribution of the gifts differently in each (1 Corinthians 12:11), so that, as he says, just as this coarse body from the earth is made up of parts, so too Christ, or rather his body, that is, the Church, has its most perfect structure through a great multitude of saints joined into a spiritual unity (1 Corinthians 12:12, 27). For this reason the inspired David too says that she is clothed “in a garment woven with gold,” embroidered in many colors (Psalm 45:9), signifying by this, I think, how many and how precious the gifts are.

Because, then, those who were to lead the world under the sun into the mysteries were to speak the saving proclamation of the Gospel to every tongue and every nation, he gave them the tongues as a sign. Men of Galilee they were, brought up in Judea, Hebrews born of Hebrews (Acts 2:7; Philippians 3:5), and yet to Medes and Parthians, and indeed to Elamites (Acts 2:9)…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74, Fragmenta in 1 Cor (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.
The section opens mid-sentence, continuing “But the workings of miracles as well, that is…” at the end of the previous section.
Cyril takes the “faith” of 1 Corinthians 12:9 as steadfastness in every good and in God’s will, not only belief that God is one.
Moses is called ἱεροφάντης, the one who reveals sacred things; rendered “the revealer of holy things.”

“Given to the believers of that time … as a sign”: the Greek puts “to the believers” at the end of the clause. It is read with “given,” since in 1 Corinthians 14:22 tongues are a sign for unbelievers; it could also be read “a sign to the believers.”
The prophetic oracle is Isaiah 28:11–12 as Paul quotes it in 1 Corinthians 14:21.
“A garment woven with gold” is Psalm 45:9 (Psalm 44:10 in the Greek numbering).
“Hebrews born of Hebrews” borrows Paul’s phrase in Philippians 3:5.
The section ends in the middle of the list of nations from Acts 2:9–11; the list continues in the next section.
